label: Computing History and Foundations
blurb: A focused six-fact drill set for Computing History and Foundations.

topics.title: Abacus
topics.hook: An abacus is a manual calculating frame used for arithmetic in several ancient civilizations.
topics.explainer: An abacus is a manual calculating frame used for arithmetic in several ancient civilizations. It is a useful TCS Quiz recall point because questions often test the term, person, date, or application together.

connections.fact: The abacus represents calculation performed by manipulating a physical aid, while Lovelace described how a machine could follow a written sequence of operations.
Both perform arithmetic, but the abacus is manually operated whereas ENIAC used electronic vacuum-tube circuits for general-purpose computation.

topics.title: Ada Lovelace
topics.hook: Ada Lovelace published notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and described an algorithm for it.
topics.explainer: Ada Lovelace published notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and described an algorithm for it. It is a useful TCS Quiz recall point because questions often test the term, person, date, or application together.

connections.fact: Lovelace published an algorithm for Babbage's proposed machine; Turing later formalised what it means for a machine to carry out any computable algorithm.
Lovelace wrote instructions for a mechanical Analytical Engine a century before ENIAC demonstrated large-scale electronic general-purpose computing.

topics.title: Alan Turing
topics.hook: Alan Turing proposed the universal Turing machine, a foundational model of computation.
topics.explainer: Alan Turing proposed the universal Turing machine, a foundational model of computation. It is a useful TCS Quiz recall point because questions often test the term, person, date, or application together.

connections.fact: Lovelace supplied an early published machine algorithm, while Turing supplied a mathematical model for universal computation.
Turing's universal machine was an abstract model; ENIAC was a physical electronic computer built in the following decade.

topics.title: ENIAC
topics.hook: ENIAC, completed in 1945, was among the first general-purpose electronic digital computers.
topics.explainer: ENIAC, completed in 1945, was among the first general-purpose electronic digital computers. It is a useful TCS Quiz recall point because questions often test the term, person, date, or application together.

connections.fact: ENIAC relied on thousands of vacuum tubes; the transistor soon made computers smaller, cooler, more reliable, and less power-hungry.

connections.relationship: From room-sized machine to dense chips
connections.fact: ENIAC illustrates early electronic scale, while Moore's Law describes the later growth in transistor density that drove miniaturisation.

topics.title: Transistor
topics.hook: The transistor was invented at Bell Labs in 1947 and replaced many vacuum-tube functions.
topics.explainer: The transistor was invented at Bell Labs in 1947 and replaced many vacuum-tube functions. It is a useful TCS Quiz recall point because questions often test the term, person, date, or application together.

connections.fact: ENIAC typifies vacuum-tube computing, and transistors replaced the same switching and amplification functions in later machines.
Moore's Law tracks the rising number of transistors that manufacturers can place on an integrated circuit.

topics.title: Moore's Law
topics.hook: Moore's Law is Gordon Moore's observation that chip transistor counts historically doubled roughly every two years.
topics.explainer: Moore's Law is Gordon Moore's observation that chip transistor counts historically doubled roughly every two years. It is a useful TCS Quiz recall point because questions often test the term, person, date, or application together.

connections.fact: The observation concerns transistor counts on chips, so the transistor is the physical unit behind the trend.
Comparing ENIAC's room-sized vacuum-tube design with modern chips makes the density trend described by Moore's Law concrete.

questions.q: Which calculating aid works by moving counters along rods or grooves?
questions.explanation: An abacus represents numbers with movable counters and supports manual arithmetic; it does not execute a stored program.

questions.q: Ada Lovelace's celebrated algorithm appeared in notes about which proposed machine?
questions.explanation: Lovelace annotated Menabrea's account of Babbage's Analytical Engine and described a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers.

questions.q: Put these milestones in chronological order: Turing's universal-machine paper, ENIAC completion, transistor invention.
questions.explanation: Turing published the model in 1936, ENIAC was completed in 1945, and Bell Labs demonstrated the transistor in 1947.

questions.q: A quiz clue says "general-purpose electronic computer completed in 1945." Which answer fits best?
questions.explanation: ENIAC is the expected 1945 general-purpose electronic-computer answer; the Analytical Engine remained unbuilt and the Manchester Baby ran later.

questions.q: An engineer replaces a vacuum-tube switch with a smaller solid-state device invented at Bell Labs in 1947. What is it?
questions.explanation: The Bell Labs transistor could switch and amplify electronically without the bulk and heat of a vacuum tube.

questions.q: What quantity did Gordon Moore originally track when formulating the observation called Moore's Law?
questions.explanation: Moore examined component density on integrated circuits; the familiar shorthand later focuses on transistor counts, not clock speed.

questions.q: Which comparison between an abacus and ENIAC is accurate?
options: Only the abacus used vacuum tubes
The abacus is manually operated; ENIAC used electronic circuits
questions.explanation: The abacus depends on human manipulation of counters, whereas ENIAC automated arithmetic with electronic vacuum-tube circuitry.

options: Alan Turing — invention of the transistor
questions.explanation: Lovelace's notes included an Analytical Engine procedure for Bernoulli numbers, an early published machine algorithm.

questions.q: A statement calls Turing the builder of ENIAC. What is the correction?
options: He proposed a mathematical model of universal computation
questions.explanation: Turing's key link here is the universal Turing machine, a theoretical model; Eckert and Mauchly led ENIAC's construction.

questions.q: Which development most directly makes Moore's Law meaningful?
options: Increasing the number of vacuum tubes per machine
questions.explanation: The observation describes repeated increases in how densely semiconductor manufacturers integrate transistors, enabling greater computing capability per chip.
